title: Whisky and Cheese Pairing | Craft Beer School
desc: Whisky and cheese pairing: why fat and salt help, five reliable matches, Indian cheeses worth trying and how to serve them in a warm kitchen.
teaser: Fat softens alcohol and salt brings out sweetness. That is why whisky and cheese work so well together.
standfirst: Wine and cheese is the famous pairing. Whisky and cheese can be better, because whisky's sweetness and intensity stand up to strong cheese. Here is how to match them and how to run a small tasting.
sections: Fat and salt are whisky's friends

Cheese brings two things that help whisky. Fat coats the tongue and softens the burn of alcohol. Salt suppresses bitterness and makes sweet flavours seem sweeter. Together they tame a strong spirit and bring its sweeter, fruitier side forward.

The other rule is intensity. A mild cheese vanishes next to a heavily peated whisky. A pungent blue overwhelms a light, floral malt. Match strength with strength and delicate with delicate, then look for flavours that echo or contrast.
Five reliable pairings to start with

• Aged cheddar with a sherry cask malt. Nutty, savoury cheese against dried fruit and spice.
  • Parmesan style hard cheese with bourbon. Salt and crunchy crystals against vanilla and caramel.
  • Blue cheese with a rich, sweet whisky or a peated malt. Sweetness tames the blue; smoke stands up to it.
  • Soft, bloomy rind cheese with a light Irish whiskey or gentle Speyside malt. Creamy against fruity.
  • Smoked cheese with a peated whisky. Smoke on smoke, best in small bites.

These are starting points, not rules. Your own palate decides.

Bandel, the small smoked and salty cheese from Bengal, is a natural match for a peated malt. Kalimpong cheese, a small, tangy cheese from the hills of north Bengal, has a gentle bite that suits a lighter whisky. A growing number of Indian artisan cheesemakers now produce aged and washed rind cheeses that are worth exploring.

Plain paneer is too mild to say much next to whisky. Fried and spiced paneer is a different story; our guide to whisky and Indian food covers that territory.
Temperature matters in an Indian kitchen

Cheese straight from the fridge tastes muted. In a cool climate you would take it out 30 to 60 minutes before serving. At 30 °C, 15 to 20 minutes is often enough; leave it longer and soft cheese starts to sweat and slump.

Cut the cheese while it is cold, plate it, cover it loosely and let it come up gently. Serve it on a cool plate away from the stove or a sunny window. Bring out a second plate later rather than leaving everything out for the evening.

Keep it small: three or four whiskies at 15 to 20 ml each, plus a few cheeses. Order the whiskies from light to heavy, with peated ones last because smoke lingers. Taste the whisky, take a small bite of cheese, then taste the whisky again. Note what changed.

Put out water, plain crackers or bread and spit cups for anyone who wants them. Make sure guests have a way home that does not involve driving. Our guide to hosting a whisky tasting at home covers the rest of the set-up.
What to put on the board

Beyond cheese, a few extras make the tasting more useful. Plain crackers or sliced baguette give a neutral base. Dried apricots or figs bridge to sherry cask whiskies. Walnuts and almonds echo the nutty notes in many aged malts. A little honey is lovely with blue cheese and a bourbon.

Keep the extras simple and few. The aim is to taste the whisky and cheese, not to build a buffet. Avoid anything very spicy, such as chilli pickle, on the same board. It will dull your palate for everything that follows.

When a pairing goes wrong, it is usually for one of two reasons. Either one side overwhelms the other, or the two clash on bitterness. A very tannic, heavily oaked whisky next to a salty, sharp cheese can taste harsh and drying.

Sweetness can also clash. A very sweet whisky with a mild, creamy cheese can feel cloying, with nothing to cut through it. A little acidity helps, which is why a sharp aged cheese often works better than a soft, buttery one with rich whiskies.

Do not be afraid of a miss. A pairing that does not work teaches you as much about your own palate as one that does, as long as you can say why.
Start with one whisky and three cheeses

For a first try, pick one whisky you know well. Buy three cheeses of very different strength: one mild, one aged and hard, one blue or smoked. Taste the whisky with each in turn and write one line about what happened.

You will quickly see which direction your whisky prefers. Next time, keep the winning cheese and change the whisky.
faqs: What cheese goes best with whisky?
Aged hard cheeses such as cheddar are the most reliable. Blue cheese suits sweet or peated whiskies; soft cheese suits lighter ones.
Does peated whisky go with cheese?
Yes, with strong flavours such as blue or smoked cheese. Mild cheeses tend to disappear next to heavy smoke.
How long should cheese sit out before serving?
In a cool room, 30 to 60 minutes. In an Indian summer kitchen, 15 to 20 minutes is often enough.
